content_groups.group_title: Q1. How do you confirm fetal death?

items: By ultrasound demonstrating absence of fetal cardiac activity. RCOG

content_groups.group_title: Q2. Can you diagnose IUFD using a Doppler?

blocks.text: No. Absence of a heartbeat on handheld Doppler should prompt urgent ultrasound confirmation rather than immediate diagnosis and disclosure of fetal death.

content_groups.group_title: Q3. What are important causes of stillbirth?

blocks.text: Placental insufficiency/FGR, placental abruption, hypertensive disease, diabetes, infection, fetal abnormalities/genetic conditions, cord abnormalities and maternal disease.

content_groups.group_title: Q4. What is the most important investigation of the placenta?

blocks.text: Placental examination and histopathology where indicated, because placental pathology can reveal evidence of insufficiency, abruption, infarction, thrombosis or infection.

content_groups.group_title: Q5. What maternal complication can occur with prolonged IUFD?

blocks.text: Coagulopathy/DIC, particularly with prolonged retention, although it is not inevitable.

content_groups.group_title: Q6. Does every woman with IUFD require Caesarean section?

blocks.text: No. Vaginal birth is generally preferred when clinically appropriate. Caesarean is reserved for specific maternal/obstetric indications or after informed discussion in selected circumstances.

content_groups.group_title: Q7. What if she has no bleeding, no infection and intact membranes?

blocks.text: Discuss expectant management, induction of labour and Caesarean birth, taking her preferences and clinical circumstances into account. NICE

content_groups.group_title: Q8. What if she has infection?

blocks.text: Prompt treatment of infection and delivery; NICE recommends immediate induction or Caesarean birth depending on the clinical situation. NICE

content_groups.group_title: Q10. What investigations would you offer after stillbirth?

blocks.text: Maternal investigations guided by history, placental examination, fetal examination, genetic/chromosomal testing where appropriate, and discussion of post-mortem examination.

“How would you manage a woman with confirmed IUFD?”

blocks.text: “I would first communicate the diagnosis sensitively and provide privacy, emotional support and an opportunity for her partner or chosen support person to be present. I would assess the mother's clinical condition, including vital signs, bleeding, abdominal pain, infection, pre-eclampsia and possible coagulopathy. I would obtain an appropriate history and investigations to look for a cause, including maternal blood tests, placental examination, fetal examination and genetic or post-mortem investigations where appropriate and with consent. If she is clinically well with intact membranes and no infection or bleeding, I would discuss expectant management, induction and Caesarean birth and respect her informed decision. If there is infection, bleeding or ruptured membranes requiring urgent management, I would arrange prompt delivery. I would provide appropriate analgesia and one-to-one support during labour, followed by bereavement care, postnatal review and counselling for a future pregnancy.”
That answer covers the entire station.
